title: Detectability of controlled leaks in an Andean water transmission main: A field evaluation of changepoint methods on flow and pressure signals
content:
by Holger Manuel Benavides-Muñoz, Peter Cheung

Leak detection on pumped transmission mains that cross steep terrain relies on hydraulic signals whose response to a small leak may be comparable to sensor noise. We evaluated five unsupervised methods (PELT with Bayesian and Akaike penalties, Bayesian online changepoint detection [BOCD], an OLS-CUSUM structural-break procedure and a moving-average ±3σ chart) on flow and pressure series recorded every 30 s during seven controlled leak trials (valve setting 3–5% of nominal flow) in two field campaigns on an Andean transmission main in Loja, Ecuador. Detections were compared with a chance-level reference obtained by placing the same number of changepoints at random. Relative to the preceding leak-free observations, flow decreased in all seven trials (mean −0.50%; sign test p = 0.016; placebo test p = 0.003), whereas pressure, recorded at 0.1-m resolution, showed no change (placebo p = 0.99). No single event exceeded its per-event detection threshold; the flow change was resolvable only as a seven-event mean (signal-to-noise ratio −3.3). None of the five detectors located leak onsets more often than chance (pooled p > 0.40 for every method–signal pair). The PELT variants flagged six of seven events on pressure, but at 560–960 false alarms per day and 13–33% precision. Although BOCD on pressure reached the highest average precision (0.54), its excess over the chance reference was not significant after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.14). A CUSUM tuned to the observed flow change, the optimal sequential detector for a persistent shift, would need 12–29 min to detect it at one false-alarm per day, 8–20 times the trial duration. Chance-level performance is therefore the expected outcome for 90–120-s leaks at 30-s sampling, whereas a persistent leak producing the same flow change would be detectable within tens of minutes.
